text: There's a gene called Casp twelve, and in most of the human species it doesn't work. The broken version isn't the exception. It's the default.
When bacteria get into your bloodstream, your immune system raises an alarm. Inflammation. Working Casp twelve turns that alarm down.
Which sounds useful, until the bacteria are winning.

A study in Nature compared people carrying the full-length, working version against people with the truncated one. The working version came with a blunted inflammatory response, and a higher risk of being overwhelmed by severe bacterial infection.
Somewhere along the line, the volume knob snapped off. And the people whose alarm got louder were the ones who kept going.

Today the broken version is close to universal. The working copy survives mainly in populations of African ancestry, at low frequency. A reminder that the version we call normal is often just the one that won.

Now, I could tell you a louder alarm must have a cost, and it sounds obvious. But the study I just described measured infection outcomes. It didn't hand us a tidy bill for everything else, and I'm not going to invent one to keep the pattern neat.
So when we say broken gene, notice what we're actually saying. For this one, you are the mutation.
Every trade so far has had a price you could look away from. The last one doesn't let you.
